13: What to know before you start
14: THE COLUMN THAT MOVES THE MOST MONEY IS "Price basis". US dealers list before sales tax, and the list price also leaves out freight (liftgate and inside delivery), installation and start-up; on top of that, the same model comes in different voltage and phase versions. Comparing a bare list price with a delivered, installed quote can throw your total off by thousands of dollars. Every figure this workbook adds up is pre-tax, and sales tax on equipment is calculated separately: in the US it's a cost, and it doesn't come back.
15: THE DELIVERY LEAD TIME IS A DECISION, NOT A DATA POINT. Few dealers commit to one in writing before you order, and the ones in the sheet are assumptions. But the longest lead time among what you can't open without is what sets your opening date, so the sheet calculates it, tells you which line sets it and warns you if it eats your calendar. Order first what takes longest, not what excites you most.
16: THE REFERENCE PRICE ISN'T YOUR PRICE. Eight lines carry an example price and fourteen an assumption, because production kitchen equipment is sold by quote. The green "Negotiated price" column is the only one that counts toward your totals: ask for three quotes per line and enter them here.
17: THIS WORKBOOK DOESN'T CALCULATE YOUR STARTUP COSTS. startup-cost-calculator.xlsx does that, and it also splits the investment by block and compares a takeover against a new build. Here you only compare: copy its equipment total into the green cell at the top and this sheet tells you how far you're drifting. There isn't a single formula pointing to another file: a link between workbooks breaks as soon as someone moves a folder, and then the workbook lies without warning.
18: THE CHOCOLATE TEMPERING MACHINE AND THE DECK OVEN ARE MARKED OPTIONAL on purpose. They're the two purchases people argue about most and the two most often bought when they aren't needed: they only come in if you open a bonbon line or if your bread and viennoiserie volume justifies it. That's why they stay out of the critical lead time and the comparable subtotal.
19: How often you use this workbook
20: Rhythm: EVERY WEEK from the day you choose the space until the day you open, which is when the checklist closes. After that, once a year for replacements and whenever you change suppliers. The "Suppliers" sheet stays alive: every time you negotiate new terms, note them here.
21: Where this workbook ends and the rest of the pack begins
22: The HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro runs the kitchen you ALREADY have open: temperature logs, cleaning records, the display-case allergen matrix. This workbook decides the kitchen you're going to buy, and those are two different questions. Within this pack, kitchen-capacity-and-site.xlsx tells you whether the space can handle production, startup-cost-calculator.xlsx sets out the full investment, and permits-and-licenses-checklist.xlsx chains the lead times up to your opening date. This is the one you take to the trade show and to the dealer.
